clue.text: Soldier at front seen in new drama with gun?

indicators.note: in places one thing within another, so a piece goes into the middle of the rest
making something new means remaking it, so these letters come out in a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of seen

explanation.surface: A soldier is cast as the lead in a new play involving a firearm.
explanation.walkthrough: The single letter goes into the middle of the rearranged letters, not at either end. The question mark admits a guardsman need not star in a play.
explanation.definitionFit: A guardsman is a soldier serving in one of the regiments of guards, such as the Household Division.

clue.text: Old dons playing golf with lead in American Gangster

indicators.note: playing with things means moving them about freely, so the letters get rearranged

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Retired academics are out on the golf course with someone playing a part in the film American Gangster.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make American Gangster look like the 2007 film title, but here it is just a description of a US mobster. Dons look like university lecturers, though mafia bosses are dons too.
explanation.definitionFit: A goodfella is slang for a member of the Mafia, popularised by the Scorsese film about New York mobsters.

clue.text: Terrible in-law: fulsome to some degree

indicators.note: only to some degree means partly, so just part of the run of letters is used

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A dreadful in-law who lays on the praise rather too thickly.
explanation.walkthrough: Ignore the hyphen, colon and space: the letters run straight on from in-law into fulsome.
explanation.definitionFit: Terrible and awful are everyday synonyms, both meaning extremely bad or unpleasant.

clue.text: Hating diets, gent goes on a bender

indicators.note: something bent is twisted out of shape, so the letters are pulled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man fed up with dieting gives up and heads out for a long drinking binge.
explanation.walkthrough: A bender is a drinking spree in the surface, but a bend is also a twist, which is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To detest is to loathe strongly, so detesting and hating are near synonyms of intense dislike.

clue.text: Overheating old server core men refurbished

indicators.note: refurbishing something rebuilds it, so the letters are reassembled differently

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An old computer server is running hot, so its core is being rebuilt by technicians.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about IT hardware; the server is really a tennis player who serves, and overheating describes his famous on-court temper tantrums.
explanation.definitionFit: John McEnroe, the retired American tennis champion, was notorious for his hot-headed outbursts at umpires.

clue.text: Husband taking down trousers will make love

indicators.note: to trouser something is to pocket it, so one piece is tucked inside another

parts.note: to take something down is to note it in writing
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A husband drops his trousers, ready for romance.
explanation.walkthrough: Trousers is a verb here, meaning pockets, not the garment. Love is nothing in tennis scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis a score of zero is called love, so love can stand for nil or nought.

clue.text: One punching fat landowner north of the border

indicators.note: a punch drives into something, so one piece is pushed inside another

parts.note: lard is pig fat
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone throws a punch at an overweight Scottish estate owner.
explanation.walkthrough: North of the border means Scotland to an English reader.
explanation.definitionFit: Laird is the Scottish word for the owner of a large country estate, the equivalent of an English lord of the manor.

clue.text: Line snorted by Joely Richardson

indicators.note: something snorted is taken inside, so the run of letters sits within these words

parts.note: the letters straddle the end of the first name and the start of the surname

explanation.surface: The actress Joely Richardson is pictured taking a line of cocaine.
explanation.walkthrough: Line looks like a line of drugs in the surface, but it means a line of a song.
explanation.definitionFit: A lyric is a single line or the words of a song, so one sung line can be called a lyric.

clue.text: Working from home, having laugh with Romeo on loch

indicators.note: one thing on another in a down clue sits above it, so the pieces stack in sequence

parts.note: to be in is to be at home
ha is the sound of a laugh
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet
Loch Ness is the famous Scottish lake

explanation.surface: Someone working remotely from a Scottish lakeside, laughing with a lover.
explanation.walkthrough: Working from home looks like one phrase about remote work, but working is the definition and home starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse in harness is pulling a load, so the idiom means busy at one's job, still employed.

clue.text: Society girls collecting tenor's outstanding bills

indicators.note: to collect something is to gather it in, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: debs are debutantes, young women entering high society
T is the abbreviation for tenor

explanation.surface: Society girls gather up the unpaid bills a tenor has run up.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after tenor is just a link (tenor is outstanding bills), not a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Debts are sums owed and still unpaid, which is what outstanding bills means.

clue.text: Set moved with effort is not in the way

indicators.note: moving things shifts them around, so these letters change their places

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A heavy stage set has been shifted with great effort and is no longer blocking anything.
explanation.walkthrough: Way here is a road, as in highway, so not in the way means not on the road.
explanation.definitionFit: Off-street describes parking or space away from the public road, so not obstructing the carriageway.

clue.text: What stops backsliding boozer?

indicators.note: a stopper plugs a gap from inside, so one piece is lodged within another
sliding back means going backwards, so this word is written from end to start

parts.note: a boozer is British slang for a pub or bar
eh is a way of saying what? when you have not heard

explanation.surface: Someone asks what will halt a drinker's relapse into old habits.
explanation.walkthrough: Boozer is the pub here, not the drinker; but read as a whole, the clue also asks what halts a drinker's relapse, which is REHAB.
explanation.definitionFit: Rehab, short for rehabilitation, is treatment that helps an addict stay off alcohol and avoid relapsing.

clue.text: Decline essentially seen in river with rapids ultimately

definitions.text: Decline essentially seen in river with rapids ultimately

indicators.note: what is seen in something lies inside it, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: the Fal is a river in Cornwall

indicators.note: the essence of something is its heart, so only the central letter is kept

parts.note: the middle letter of the seven-letter word

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so the closing letter is taken

parts.note: the final letter of rapids

explanation.surface: A river drops sharply in the middle of its course, just after a stretch of rapids.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fal is a river in Cornwall, England. Read whole, the clue also describes the answer: a drop in a river after its rapids is a waterfall.
explanation.definitionFit: Falls are waterfalls, where a river declines steeply, often just after a stretch of rapids.

clue.text: Awful radicals on right which help some get on track?

definitions.text: which help some get on track?

indicators.note: something awful is a mess, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Dreadful political extremists tie up with the right, supposedly to set some people straight.
explanation.walkthrough: Get on track sounds like reforming one's life, but it literally means getting on a train. In Britain a railcard is a discount card for train fares.
explanation.definitionFit: Railcards give certain groups, such as students or pensioners, cheaper rail travel, so they help those people board trains.

clue.text: After bringing back posh young woman, party on

indicators.note: one thing coming after another follows it, so the pieces are set in sequence
bringing something back returns it the way it came, so it is written backwards

parts.note: gel imitates an upper-class pronunciation of girl
a side is a party or faction in a dispute

explanation.surface: Having brought a well-to-do young woman home, the party carries on.
explanation.walkthrough: On looks like a link word at the end, but it is the definition. In cricket the on side, also called the leg side, is the half of the field behind the batter's legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket uses on and leg interchangeably for the half of the field nearest the batsman's body.

clue.text: Bloomer in foreign article written by European

indicators.note: words written by others are set alongside them, so the pieces simply join up

parts.note: a German is a European
der is the German masculine definite article

explanation.surface: A gaffe turns up in a newspaper piece by a European writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Bloomer means a blunder in British English, but here it is anything that blooms. The answer reads in reverse of the clue order: the European comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Germander is a flowering plant of the mint family, so it is a bloomer in the sense of a thing that flowers.

clue.text: Atheistic track rejected by the French Elvis in the end

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so this word is turned round

parts.note: to dog someone is to track or follow them
les is the French plural for the

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the final letter of Elvis

explanation.surface: A song denying God is turned down by French listeners, as is Elvis in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: Track looks like a song on an album, but it is a verb, to follow, like a hound.
explanation.definitionFit: Godless and atheistic both describe someone who does not believe in any deity.

clue.text: Might we be thus when the sun goes over the moon?

definitions.text: Might we be thus when the sun goes over the moon?

parts.words: Might we be thus when the sun goes over the moon?
parts.note: surface reading: how would we feel during a solar eclipse, when the sun and moon line up?

parts.words: the sun goes over the moon
parts.note: setter's reading: over the moon means thrilled, and when the sun is covered we have lost our light

explanation.walkthrough: Two readings meet: over the moon is an idiom for joyful, and during an eclipse the world is literally robbed of light, so de-lighted.
explanation.definitionFit: Being over the moon means being thrilled and very happy, and a darkened world has had its light removed.

clue.text: Leading men suffering one brightening battle scene

parts.note: leading men in films are its stars
hell is great suffering

explanation.surface: Film stars endure misery while one actor lights up a war movie scene.
explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration splits STAR SHELL differently from the pieces, so the S moves across the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: A star shell is a flare fired from a gun that bursts in the air to light up a battlefield at night.

clue.text: A Republican trapped in window will be fine

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something trapped in a place is shut inside it, so one piece is enclosed by another

parts.note: a light is a pane or window
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A Republican politician stuck in a window frame insists it will all be fine.
explanation.walkthrough: Light for a window is an architectural sense, as in skylight or fanlight.
explanation.definitionFit: Alright is a common spelling of all right, meaning satisfactory or OK.

clue.text: Place head up above one's heels in Kundalini yoga

indicators.note: in a down entry one thing above another comes before it, so the pieces line up in order
in a down clue going up means reading from bottom to top, so the word is turned round

parts.note: nut is slang for head
I is one, and the 's stays as S

indicators.note: the heel is the back end of a foot, so each word gives its last letter

parts.note: the final letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A yoga instruction: put your head up above your heels in a headstand pose.
explanation.walkthrough: Place looks like a verb in the instruction, but it is a noun naming a country. Heels are the ends of the two yoga words.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunisia is a country in North Africa, and a country is a place in crossword terms.

clue.text: Lining fabric found in missiles I assess

indicators.note: something found in a place is inside it, so the letters lie within these words

parts.note: the letters run from inside the first word through the next two

explanation.surface: A defence analyst finds strange cloth packed inside the weapons being inspected.
explanation.walkthrough: Lining fabric reads like part of the hidden instruction, but it is the whole definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Silesia is a thin twilled cotton cloth used for pockets and garment linings, named after the central European region.

clue.text: A shade sad after son sat on jelly?

indicators.note: in a down clue sitting on something means resting above it, so one piece comes first
one thing after another follows it, so the pieces are put in order

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son
KY Jelly is a well-known lubricant brand
feeling blue means feeling sad

explanation.surface: A son, rather downcast, has plonked himself on a wobbly dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that jelly stands for one brand name, cut to its initials. Note the answer order differs from the clue: sad comes last.
explanation.definitionFit: Sky blue is a pale clear blue colour, one particular shade among the blues.

clue.text: A poor penalty by City's an objectionable thing

indicators.note: one thing set by another stands beside it, so the pieces join end to end

parts.note: taken as written
poor quality is bad
pen is short for penalty in football talk
NY is New York, the archetypal big city

explanation.surface: A football fan grumbles that a dodgy spot kick given to City was outrageous.
explanation.walkthrough: City looks like Manchester City in the football surface. The 's is short for is, linking wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom says a bad penny always turns up, meaning an unwelcome person or thing that keeps coming back.

clue.text: Love is about supporting a devoted other primarily

indicators.note: in a down clue a support sits underneath, so this piece goes below the others

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letters are kept

parts.note: the first letters of the two words
re means about, as in a letter heading

explanation.surface: A sentimental saying: love means standing by a faithful partner.
explanation.walkthrough: Supporting is a placement word in a down answer: the piece meaning about goes underneath. Re is the Latin-derived 'in the matter of' seen in letter headings.
explanation.definitionFit: To adore someone is to love them deeply, so the verb is a stronger synonym.

clue.text: Salesman seen around about old city is more virtuous

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece wraps another
turning around means facing the other way, so this word runs backwards

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative
Ur is the ancient city in Mesopotamia

explanation.surface: A travelling salesman tours an ancient city and becomes more saintly.
explanation.walkthrough: Ur is the crosswords' favourite old city; around and about look like a repeated word but each does its own job.
explanation.definitionFit: Pure means morally clean and chaste, so purer is the comparative for having greater virtue.

clue.text: Unpleasant people stealing fine presents

indicators.note: a thief takes something and keeps it, so one piece ends up inside another

parts.note: git is British slang for a contemptible person
F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Nasty people make off with some lovely presents.
explanation.walkthrough: Presents looks like a verb after the subject, but it is the plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Gifts and presents are things given freely to someone, the two words being everyday synonyms.

clue.text: France isn't commonly weak

parts.note: F is the international vehicle code for France
ain't is the colloquial form of isn't

explanation.surface: A sneer that France is not usually feeble.
explanation.walkthrough: Commonly marks a non-standard form of speech rather than frequency.
explanation.definitionFit: Faint can mean lacking strength or barely perceptible, as in a feeble voice.

clue.text: Military command in Band of Brothers?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an instruction issued by an officer
second meaning: a religious community of monks or friars

explanation.surface: Spotting a military order given in the television war drama Band of Brothers.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics dress the second definition up as the TV series about American paratroopers; read plainly it is a group of religious brothers.
explanation.definitionFit: A command from an officer is an order, and a monastic fraternity such as the Franciscans is also an order.

clue.text: Very literary song first appearing in electronic game

parts.note: so means very, as in so good
lit is short for literary or literature
an air is a tune or song

indicators.note: what appears first is the opening letter, so only that one is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of electronic

explanation.surface: A highbrow tune is used for the first time in a video game.
explanation.walkthrough: Electronic game looks like one phrase, but electronic only supplies a letter and game alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Solitaire is a card or peg game played by one person, now also familiar on computers.

clue.text: Fear losing knight finally is a blunder

indicators.note: to lose something is to be without it, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: terror is extreme fear

indicators.note: finally points to the very end, so only the last letter is wanted

parts.note: the final letter of knight

explanation.surface: A chess player panics at losing a knight and realises it was a howler.
explanation.walkthrough: Knight looks like the chess piece and its usual N, but here it supplies its last letter, T, which comes off the front.
explanation.definitionFit: An error is a mistake, and a blunder is a careless or stupid mistake.

clue.text: According to hearsay, cat on lead needs training

indicators.note: training reshapes behaviour, so the letters are drilled into a new form

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Word has it that a cat being walked on a leash needs schooling.
explanation.walkthrough: According to hearsay sounds like a framing phrase, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Anecdotal evidence rests on personal stories passed around rather than proper research, so it amounts to hearsay.
